newsitem.title: UK: Europe can't match US economy but markets march on.
newsitem.headline: Europe can't match US economy but markets march on.

text.p: European financial markets were swift to take their cue from the United States on Wednesday after Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan spoke of modest inflation and fundamental shifts in the economy.

But economists said Europe's knee-jerk bullish reaction, while warranted in the short term, did not tally completely with the underlying economic situation, where structural reform was well behind the U.S.
"You're talking years, rather than quarters," said Robin Marshall, chief economist at Chase in London.
"The Fed has implicitly recognised that the supply side of the economy has changed. The problem is in the economy here the structural adjustment hasn't happened."

U.S. stock and bond markets roared ahead after Greenspan said Fed policymakers were "reasonably confident" inflation would be quite modest this year and proclaimed the economy was undergoing "basic improvements" as technology boosted productivity.

In other words, the U.S. has been able to enjoy a long period of growth with relatively minimal inflation because companies are able to increase margins without passing on price increases to consumers.

Blue chip stocks rose nearly two percent on Tuesday, and the 30-year U.S. long bond climbed more than a point and a half. Stock indices throughout Europe duly followed and German, French and British bond markets also rose to new highs.
"The positive tone is going to continue," said Sonja Gibbs, senior bond strategist at Nomura International in London.

"But I think maybe over the next several weeks there's likely to be a growing realisation that Europe is on the upswing," she said, noting the increased interest rate and inflationary pressure that went with that.
"There's not necessarily this new paradigm of continued growth and low inflation."

For more than a year, international markets have been watching every twist and turn in the U.S. economy for any signs that inflation would bubble up again. Time and time again the data in the U.S. said otherwise.
Europe too has little sign of inflation, thanks in part to the various economic straitjackets imposed by Maastricht criteria.

But with the exception of Britain, there is also little sign of vibrant growth. The powerhouse of European economies, Germany, is expected to show growth of just 2.2 percent this year, according to the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development.
Gibbs said Europe structurally speaking could be as much as 10-15 years behind the U.S.
"It's a whole spectrum of things. You need businesses to have enough confidence to make the heavy investments in productivity improvements. You need much better developed service sectors."
She said many economies were still heavily depenedent on manufacturing and agriculture, but it was in areas such as services that flexible, low-inflation job creation could be achieved.
But Paul Horne, chief international economist Smith Barney in Paris, said the impression that all of Europe has not embarked on the path to low-inflation productivity is not completely accurate.
"Nobody ever talks about little Europe," he said.
Countries such as Finland and Ireland were excellent examples of economies that had made fundamental shifts toward robust growth without stirring inflation.
Britain is in another league in terms of size but it too has embraced U.S.-style reform and is reaping some of the rewards, analysts said.
"Then you have the other Europe which is led by the two economic giants and their satellites. Germany and France are the ones that are not biting the entitlement bullets," Horne said.
"There is an entitlement addiction and a job protectionist framework which takes total precedence over job creation. It is Europe's big problem and it will continue to be."
Nevertheless, with interest rates at historically low levels all around Europe and ample liquidity, markets are paying scant attention at the moment to long-term structural issues.
For the time being, analysts said, dealers are more than happy to mark prices higher whenever the U.S. does.
